title: How to Respond to Reply-All Corrections Gracefully
summary: Former Duke and Columbia communication teacher Dorie Clark explains how to handle public corrections over email. Rather than giving long explanations or apologies, she recommends using the Good Catch Technique to remain gracious and professional.
key_points: Avoid giving long explanations (e.g., 'So sorry, I pulled that from last month's file'), as it makes you look more concerned with protecting your reputation than with accuracy.
Do not apologize or over-explain, as doing so inflates the issue and draws unnecessary attention to the mistake.
Use the Good Catch Technique: reply to all with a simple thank you and the corrected material (e.g., 'Good catch, thank you. I've fixed page three and the corrected report is attached.').
Fixing errors publicly and calmly neutralizes any attempts to make you look bad while showing everyone that you are gracious, non-defensive, and open to learning.
content:
Post text:
Here’s what to say when someone corrects you on reply-all. They *should* have just replied to you, but they chose to make your mistake public, and now you have to correct it. And keep your reputation intact! I taught communication at Duke and Columbia, and this strategy can help. Follow me for more on becoming a better communicator.

Transcript:
Here's what to say when someone corrects you on reply-all without getting defensive. You've just sent a report to the whole team and a colleague replies to everyone, "Actually, the number on page three is wrong." They could have just sent that to you, but they chose to do it in front of everyone to put you in your place. I taught communication at Duke and Columbia and here is what to say. Most people write back with a long explanation: "So sorry, I pulled that from last month's file." They want everyone to know that they weren't being careless. But a long explanation looks like you care more about protecting your reputation than about accuracy. Instead, use what I call the Good Catch Technique. Here's how it works. You reply to everyone with a thank you and the correction. "Good catch, thank you. I've fixed page three and the corrected report is attached." Note what you're not doing, which is apologizing or explaining. That makes the issue bigger than it should be and it draws too much attention to it. Instead, the Good Catch Technique works because you've taken their correction calmly. You fix things in front of the same people who saw the mistake. If your colleague was trying to make you look bad, it didn't work because you were gracious and not defensive. And if they were trying to help, you've shown that you're willing to learn. So the next time someone corrects you in front of everyone on reply-all, try the Good Catch Technique and follow me for more on becoming a better communicator.
